reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / WHO guidance on filariasis
clinicalPearls: Caused by the filarial nematode Loa loa, transmitted by the day-biting Chrysops (mango or deer) fly in the rainforests of West and Central Africa

The classic features are transient, localised, non-pitting angio-oedematous 'Calabar swellings', often around joints, and the sensation or sight of an adult worm migrating across the subconjunctiva of the eye
Peripheral eosinophilia is typically prominent, and symptoms are often more marked in expatriates and visitors than in endemic residents
Diagnosis rests on detecting sheathed microfilariae with daytime (midday) periodicity on a stained blood film, reflecting the vector's daytime biting
Adult worms may be identified during their migration across the eye or under the skin
Treatment options include diethylcarbamazine (which targets microfilariae and adult worms) and albendazole, with careful attention to microfilarial load
High Loa loa microfilarial loads carry a risk of severe encephalopathy when treated with certain antifilarial drugs, so the burden must be assessed before therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Loiasis is caused by infection with the filarial worm Loa loa. Infective larvae are deposited when an infected Chrysops fly takes a blood meal; the larvae mature into adult worms that migrate through subcutaneous and connective tissues over years. Adult females release sheathed microfilariae that circulate in the peripheral blood with a diurnal periodicity matching the daytime feeding of the vector, allowing onward transmission. Host immune and hypersensitivity responses to migrating adults and their products produce the transient inflammatory Calabar swellings and eosinophilia, while migration across the bulbar conjunctiva gives the classic 'eye worm'. Heavy microfilaraemia is largely asymptomatic itself but becomes clinically important because rapid microfilarial killing during treatment can trigger severe inflammatory reactions, including encephalopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of angio-oedema or urticaria
additionalInvestigations: Daytime (midday) peripheral blood film for sheathed microfilariae
Quantification of Loa loa microfilarial density before treatment
Filarial serology or antigen/antibody testing where available
Slit-lamp or direct examination if a worm is visible in the eye
Molecular (PCR) assays for species confirmation where accessible
redFlags: Very high microfilarial load, given the risk of treatment-associated encephalopathy
Neurological deterioration or encephalopathy during antifilarial therapy
Renal involvement or severe systemic hypersensitivity reactions
reference.prognosis: Loiasis is generally a chronic, non-fatal infection with a good prognosis when managed carefully; the principal danger is treatment-related severe reactions, especially encephalopathy in heavily microfilaraemic individuals.
pitfalls: Starting antifilarial treatment without first measuring the microfilarial load and considering encephalopathy risk
Timing the diagnostic blood film incorrectly and missing the daytime-periodic microfilariae
Co-treating without recognising overlap with onchocerciasis or lymphatic filariasis in co-endemic regions
Attributing Calabar swellings to simple allergy in a returning traveller
management: Give diethylcarbamazine as definitive therapy targeting microfilariae and adult worms, but only after quantifying microfilarial density
Reduce heavy microfilaraemia first with albendazole or apheresis to lower the risk of treatment-related encephalopathy
Avoid or use extreme caution with ivermectin and diethylcarbamazine in high microfilarial loads because of severe post-treatment reactions
Remove an adult worm surgically or mechanically when it migrates across the conjunctiva or subcutis and is accessible
Monitor closely during treatment for encephalopathy and other reactions, providing supportive care
Advise vector-avoidance measures against the day-biting Chrysops fly
Involve tropical medicine or infectious diseases specialists and consider repeat courses given relapse
